docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Elastic, internal-strain and piezoelectric tensors from the fewest possible stress calculations, for every crystal symmetry and with any electronic-structure code.

minelastic implements the minimal and uncoupled strain sets scheme of S. I. Simak and U. Singh, arXiv:2610.11733 (2026). Each independent elastic constant is read off one stress component of one strained cell, and the number of strain patterns is the smallest that any stress-strain method can use: one for a cubic crystal and two for tetragonal, trigonal and hexagonal crystals, where the usual approach applies six. The constants agree with those of the six single strains to a few hundredths of a GPa.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from ase.build import bulk
from ase.calculators.emt import EMT
import minelastic

result = minelastic.calculate(bulk("Cu", "fcc", a=3.59, cubic=True), EMT())
print(result.summary())

Any ASE calculator works the same way. For DFT codes, minelastic writes the input files of the strained cells and reads the finished calculations:

# run VASP in every directory listed in el/STATES
minelastic collect el

docs.title: What it computes
docs.text:
quantity calculations beyond the strained cells guide elastic constants, bulk and shear moduli, stability none Elastic constants in practice internal-strain tensor none: the forces of the same cells Internal strain clamped-ion piezoelectric tensor none: Berry phase in the same cells Piezoelectricity relaxed-ion elastic constants relaxations, or single points with displaced atoms Relaxed-ion constants Born charges, total piezoelectric tensors e and d single points with displaced atoms Piezoelectricity elastic constants at finite temperature, with error bars one MD run per strained cell Finite temperature

The symmetry analysis includes magnetic order (Magnetic materials). Every quantity is built on the same strained cells, so each inherits the saving of the minimal set (Cost).

docs.title: Supported codes
docs.text: minelastic writes the inputs for VASP and Quantum ESPRESSO from a template of the relaxed structure, and for ABINIT, FHI-aims and every structure format that ASE can write (CASTEP, SIESTA, ...). Any ASE calculator, such as EMT, MACE or CP2K, is used directly from Python. There are tutorials for VASP, Quantum ESPRESSO, ABINIT and CP2K, with the output of real calculations.

docs.title: How this documentation is organized
docs.text:
If you are new to minelastic, start with the installation and your first elastic tensor, which needs no DFT code, and then the tutorial for your code. The how-to guides treat each quantity and each code in more depth. The theory section has the method and all formulas; you do not need it to use minelastic. The reference documents the Python API, the command line, units and conventions, and the validation against VASP, Quantum ESPRESSO, ABINIT and CP2K.

If you use minelastic in published work, please cite the paper (Citing).

docs.title: ASE calculators
docs.text: Any ASE calculator that returns the stress can be used directly from Python: EMT and other interatomic potentials, machine-learned potentials such as MACE, and DFT codes driven through ASE such as CP2K. The first tutorial uses EMT, and the CP2K tutorial a DFT code.

docs.title: calculate
docs.text:
result = minelastic.calculate(atoms, calc, relax_ions=False, method="uncoupled", fmax=1e-4, steps=500,
                              optimizer=None, dipole=None, **setup_kwargs)

builds the strain set of atoms (ElasticSetup(atoms, **setup_kwargs)), computes every strained and displaced cell with the ASE calculator calc and returns the ElasticResult. For each cell it takes

  • the stress, calc.get_stress() in eV/Å\(^3\), converted to GPa (tension positive, as in ASE);
  • the forces, for the internal-strain tensor and, with ionic=True, the force constants;
  • the dipole dipole(atoms) in e Å, if a function is given, for the Born charges and the piezoelectric tensors.

With relax_ions=True the atoms of each strained cell are first relaxed at fixed cell with optimizer (default BFGS) to fmax (eV/Å). setup_kwargs are the options of ElasticSetup: scheme, delta, stencil, symprec, frame, ionic and displacement (Python API).

The how-to pages show each quantity with an ASE calculator:

Tip

Relax the reference cell with the same calculator first: the textbook constants refer to a stress-free reference.

docs.title: Machine-learned potentials
docs.text:
Any ASE calculator works.

Double precision

Run machine-learned potentials in double precision: the stresses of the strained cells differ by only about 1 GPa.

from ase.io import read
from ase.filters import FrechetCellFilter
from ase.optimize import BFGS
from mace.calculators import mace_mp
import minelastic

atoms = read("POSCAR")
calc = mace_mp(model="medium", default_dtype="float64")
atoms.calc = calc
BFGS(FrechetCellFilter(atoms)).run(fmax=1e-4)           # stress-free reference
result = minelastic.calculate(atoms, calc, relax_ions=True)
print(result.summary())

For wurtzite AlN with MACE-MPA-0, the minimal set and the six single strains agree to 0.1 GPa, and the two routes to the relaxed-ion constants to 0.3 GPa (Validation).

docs.title: ABINIT
docs.text:
A complete example is the ABINIT tutorial. The template directory holds the reference structure as POSCAR and one ABINIT input file (*.abi) that reads it with structure "poscar:POSCAR". The input sets everything else: pseudopotentials in the order of the POSCAR species, cutoff, k-point mesh and convergence.

ABINIT's POSCAR reader takes the element of each atom from the end of its coordinate line, so minelastic writes the strained POSCARs in that form; for the same reason two species of one element cannot be used. Magnetic sublattices are set with spinat, which minelastic also reads for the symmetry (Magnetic materials). collect reads the stress and forces from the newest *.abo file of each directory. With --relax-ions, ionmov 2, ntime 100 and tolmxf 1.0d-6 are appended unless the input sets ionmov. The cell must stay fixed (optcell 0), the ions must stay fixed for clamped-ion runs (no ionmov), and dataset-specific values of ionmov and optcell are not accepted.

docs.title: FHI-aims
docs.text:
The template directory holds geometry.in (the reference structure) and control.in:

minelastic generate aims ref/ -o el          # geometry.in per strain state, control.in copied
# run aims in every directory, output in aims.out
minelastic collect el

control.in must request the stress (compute_analytical_stress .true.) and must not relax the cell (relax_unit_cell); otherwise generate stops with an error. For clamped ions it must not relax the atoms either. With --relax-ions, relax_geometry bfgs 1E-3 is added unless it is present. The FHI-aims reader is tested on an output distributed with ASE; minelastic has not been run with FHI-aims itself.

docs.title: Any format ASE can write (CASTEP, SIESTA, ...)
docs.text:
The generic interface writes only the strained structure in each directory and copies further input files. The results are read back with ASE:

minelastic generate generic crystal.cell -o el --format castep-cell --filename crystal.cell \
    --extra crystal.param
# run the code in every directory
minelastic collect el --output crystal.castep --format castep-castep

The reference structure (crystal.cell here) is read with the same --format as the files that are written. Make sure the inputs request the stress and keep the cell fixed. Keep the ions fixed too, unless you want relaxed ions. minelastic info crystal.cell --format castep-cell shows the strain set first.

docs.title: Anything else
docs.text: The Python API separates the strain set from how the calculations are run, so stresses from any source can be used (Your own workflow).

docs.title: Quantum ESPRESSO
docs.text: A complete example is the Quantum ESPRESSO tutorial. Below we describe how minelastic handles the pw.x inputs and outputs.

docs.title: Template and commands
docs.text:
The template is the pw.x input of the relaxed reference structure. pw.x runs in one sub-directory per state, so set pseudo_dir to an absolute path.

minelastic generate qe pw.in -o el                  # clamped ions
minelastic generate qe pw.in -o el_relaxed --relax-ions
for d in $(cat el/STATES); do (cd el/$d && mpirun pw.x -in pw.in > pw.out); done
minelastic collect el

docs.title: The inputs
docs.text:
Every strained input is written with

  • ibrav = 0, the strained CELL_PARAMETERS in Å and ATOMIC_POSITIONS crystal;
  • the species labels and if_pos flags of the template;
  • tstress and tprnfor switched on.

Any ibrav is accepted, with celldm or with A, B, C, cosAB, ..., and the positions may be given in alat, bohr, angstrom or crystal. All other namelists and cards are copied unchanged. For relaxed ions, calculation = 'relax' is set, with tight forc_conv_thr and etot_conv_thr unless the template sets them: the defaults of pw.x stop the relaxation before the internal strain is relaxed. collect reads pw.out in each directory (--output for another name). pw.x prints the stress in Ry/bohr\(^3\), positive in compression; minelastic converts it to GPa, positive in tension.

docs.title: Magnetic order and molecular dynamics
docs.text: pw.x needs a separate species label for every magnetic sublattice (starting magnetization per species), and minelastic treats the labels as distinct species in the symmetry analysis. With noncolin = .true. it also reads the moment directions from starting_magnetization, angle1 and angle2 (Magnetic materials). For finite temperature, the template has calculation = 'md' with a thermostat in &IONS and a fixed cell; generate --md keeps it and collect --md averages the stresses of all steps (Finite temperature).

docs.title: VASP
docs.text: A complete example is the VASP tutorial. Below we describe how minelastic handles the VASP inputs and outputs.

docs.title: Template and commands
docs.text:
The template directory holds the input of the relaxed reference structure: POSCAR, INCAR, POTCAR, and KPOINTS or KSPACING in the INCAR.

minelastic info --code vasp ref/             # symmetry, tensor form and strain set; no files written
minelastic generate vasp ref/ -o el          # one directory per state, listed in el/STATES
minelastic collect el                        # after the runs; writes el/elastic.json

Each el/<state>/ holds POSCAR (the strained or displaced cell, with the species lines and the selective-dynamics flags of the template), INCAR, KPOINTS and POTCAR (--potcar link symlinks it). el/minelastic.json records the setup; collect needs it.

docs.title: The INCAR
docs.text:
generate copies the template's INCAR and changes only what the type of calculation requires:

  • IBRION = -1, NSW = 0, ISIF = 2 for clamped ions (ISIF = 2 computes the stress);
  • IBRION = 2, NSW = 99, ISIF = 2 and, unless set, EDIFFG = -5E-4 with --relax-ions;
  • with --md, the template's IBRION = 0, NSW and POTIM are kept and ISIF = 2 is set;
  • NFREE, POTIM, LEPSILON and LCALCEPS are removed, so that an IBRION = 6 input can be used as it is (relaxations then use VASP's default POTIM);
  • KSPACING is replaced by the explicit k-point mesh of the reference cell, so that all cells use the same mesh.

Every change is listed. The settings that matter for stress differences of a few GPa are checked, but left as they are: EDIFF at most 1E-6 (1E-8 suggested; 1E-6 for MD), ENCUT at least 1.3 times the largest ENMAX of the POTCAR, PREC = Accurate (or High) and LREAL = .FALSE.. The template of the tutorial meets all of them. The INCAR of an IBRION = 6 run with VASP's defaults gives:

$ cat ibrion6/INCAR
IBRION = 6
ISIF = 3
NFREE = 2
POTIM = 0.015
$ minelastic generate vasp ibrion6 -o el
...
NOTE: INCAR: set IBRION = -1 (template: 6), NSW = 0, ISIF = 2 (template: 3); removed NFREE, POTIM
NOTE: INCAR: recommended for small stress differences: EDIFF default 1E-4 -> 1E-8, ENCUT default ENMAX = 400 -> 520, PREC default Normal -> Accurate. The template values are kept; --fix-incar (fix_incar=True) applies all of these

--fix-incar applies all of the recommended values. There is no partial fix: the INCAR is either the template's or follows all the recommendations.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
Any scheduler works. For example, a Slurm job array over the lines of STATES:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --array=1-8              # one task per line of el/STATES
d=el/$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" el/STATES)
cd "$d" && srun vasp_std > out

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
collect reads the stress and the forces of each directory from vasprun.xml, or from OUTCAR if there is no readable vasprun.xml. VASP prints the stress in kB, positive in compression, in the order XX YY ZZ XY YZ ZX; minelastic converts it to GPa, positive in tension, in Voigt order. With --md the stress of every ionic step is read; with --piezo the Berry-phase dipole of each cell (LCALCPOL); with --born OUTCAR the Born charges and the clamped-ion piezoelectric tensor of a DFPT (LEPSILON) or LCALCEPS run.

minelastic vasp-tensor OUTCAR reads the tensor that VASP prints for IBRION = 6 with ISIF = 3 or more, converts it to GPa and Voigt order, and adds the Voigt-Reuss-Hill moduli and the Born stability test (Elastic constants in practice).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Use the same ENCUT, PREC, k-point mesh and EDIFF for the reference and all strained cells. The plane-wave basis changes with the volume of the strained cell, and a raised cutoff (1.3 to 1.4 times ENMAX) keeps the resulting Pulay stress small.
  • MAGMOM, LDAU*, ISPIN and all other tags are copied unchanged, and MAGMOM enters the symmetry analysis (Magnetic materials). If the cell has to be rotated to its standard orientation, direction-dependent inputs (LNONCOLLINEAR, LSORBIT, SAXIS, EFIELD, Cartesian k points) are refused; use --frame input.
  • The elastic constants, the internal-strain tensor, the relaxed-ion constants and the piezoelectric tensors of the tutorial structure are on the how-to pages: elastic constants, relaxed ions, internal strain and piezoelectricity.

docs.title: First run with ABINIT
docs.text: Here we compute the five elastic constants of wurtzite AlN with ABINIT, starting from the input files of the relaxed structure. This takes four single-point calculations, 373 s in total on one 32-core node. The output shown below is from these runs.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the template
docs.text:
minelastic writes the input of every strained cell from a template: a directory with the reference structure as a POSCAR and one ABINIT input file that reads it. We use examples/abinit_aln from the repository. The input file aln.abi is

# wurtzite AlN, PBE, PseudoDojo v0.4 standard norm-conserving pseudopotentials (Al.psp8, N.psp8)
# the structure is read from POSCAR; set pp_dirpath to the directory with the pseudopotentials
structure "poscar:POSCAR"
pp_dirpath "./pseudo"
pseudos "Al.psp8, N.psp8"
ecut 48
ngkpt 8 8 5
nshiftk 1
shiftk 0 0 0
occopt 1
nstep 100
tolvrs 1.0d-18
chksymbreak 0
prtwf 0
prtden 0
prteig 0

and the POSCAR holds the structure, with the element of each atom at the end of its line, as ABINIT's POSCAR reader requires:

AlN, wurtzite, PBE (relaxed with VASP; see vasp_aln)
1.0
     3.1284000000000001    0.0000000000000000    0.0000000000000000
    -1.5641999999999994    2.7092738731992383    0.0000000000000000
     0.0000000000000000    0.0000000000000000    5.0163000000000002
Al N
2 2
Direct
   0.3333333333333333  0.6666666666666666  0.0000000000000000  Al
   0.6666666666666667  0.3333333333333334  0.4999999999999999  Al
   0.3333333333333333  0.6666666666666666  0.3817999999999999  N
   0.6666666666666667  0.3333333333333334  0.8817999999999998  N

The pseudopotentials are the PBE standard set of PseudoDojo v0.4, and the cutoff and the convergence threshold are tight.

Pseudopotential path

Every calculation runs in a directory of its own, so set pp_dirpath to the absolute path of the directory with Al.psp8 and N.psp8.

Convergence

Elastic constants are differences of stresses of a few GPa, so they are much more sensitive to the cutoff, the k-point mesh, the smearing and the convergence threshold than total energies are. The settings here are chosen to show the workflow; they are not the result of a convergence study. Before using the constants in a publication, check that they change by less than the accuracy you need when the cutoff (ecut) is raised and the k-point mesh (ngkpt) refined, and relax the reference structure with the final settings.

docs.title: 2. Look at the strain set
docs.text:
minelastic info analyses the structure without writing anything:

$ minelastic info --code abinit abinit_aln --stencil central
space group P6_3mc (186), point group 6mm, elastic type hexagonal
5 independent constants: c11, c12, c13, c33, c44
invariant strains (free lattice parameters) = minimum number of strain patterns: 2
stiffness matrix in the working frame:
          c11            c12            c13              0              0              0
          c12            c11            c13              0              0              0
          c13            c13            c33              0              0              0
            0              0              0            c44              0              0
            0              0              0              0            c44              0
            0              0              0              0              0  (c11 - c12)/2
strain set 'minimal': 2 pattern(s), step 0.01, multipliers (-1, 1)
  pattern 1: xx+yz          s1 = 1 c11, s2 = 1 c12, s3 = 1 c13, s4 = 1 c44
  pattern 2: zz             s1 = 1 c13, s2 = 1 c13, s3 = 1 c33

The crystal is hexagonal, with five independent elastic constants, and two strain patterns determine all of them. Pattern 1 stretches the cell along x and shears it in the yz plane at the same time; pattern 2 stretches it along z. The entry s1 = 1 c11 means that the first stress component of pattern 1, \(\sigma_{xx}\), equals \(c_{11}\) times the strain. Every constant appears alone in at least one stress component, so each is read off directly.

Two points per strain

By default minelastic applies each pattern at \(\pm 0.01\) and \(\pm 0.02\), which makes the numerical derivative more accurate but doubles the number of calculations. For this first run, --stencil central keeps only \(\pm 0.01\) (the multipliers -1 and 1 in the output above).

docs.title: 3. Write the inputs
docs.text:
$ minelastic generate abinit abinit_aln -o el --stencil central
...
4 calculations written to el/ (list in el/STATES)
$ cat el/STATES
s1_m1
s1_p1
s2_m1
s2_p1
$ ls el/s1_p1
POSCAR
aln.abi

generate prints the same analysis as info (left out here) and writes one directory per strained cell: s1_p1 is pattern 1 at \(+0.01\), s2_m1 pattern 2 at \(-0.01\). Each holds the strained POSCAR and a copy of the input file. The input must keep the cell and the ions fixed; generate stops with an error if it relaxes either.

docs.title: 4. Run ABINIT
docs.text:
The four calculations are independent. Run them one after another,

for d in $(cat el/STATES); do (cd el/$d && mpirun abinit aln.abi > log); done

or at the same time, for example as a Slurm job array:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --array=1-4
d=el/$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" el/STATES)
cd "$d" && srun abinit aln.abi > log

collect reads the stress of each cell from the newest *.abo file in its directory and prints:

  • the five independent constants and the full stiffness matrix, in GPa, with \(C_{66} = (c_{11} - c_{12})/2\);
  • the Born stability test: the crystal is mechanically stable if all eigenvalues of the matrix are positive;
  • the Voigt-Reuss-Hill bulk modulus K, shear modulus G and Young's modulus E, Poisson's ratio nu and the universal anisotropy index A_U;
  • a consistency check: the stress components that are not needed for the constants are compared with the values that the fitted tensor predicts. A deviation of more than a few tenths of a GPa points to an unrelaxed reference structure, loose convergence or a lower symmetry than assumed.

docs.title: 6. Use the results
docs.text:
Everything is also written to el/elastic.json:

import json

with open("el/elastic.json") as f:
    res = json.load(f)
print({name: round(value, 2) for name, value in res["constants"].items()})
print(f"bulk modulus {res['properties']['K_H']:.1f} GPa, shear modulus {res['properties']['G_H']:.1f} GPa")

{'c11': 441.69, 'c12': 94.39, 'c13': 59.2, 'c33': 434.52, 'c44': 125.84}
bulk modulus 193.6 GPa, shear modulus 156.2 GPa

res["C"] is the 6 x 6 matrix. The other entries are listed under Command line.

docs.title: 7. Check the result
docs.text:
The same calculation with the six single strains (--scheme asess, 12 cells) gives, with the same settings:

GPa c11 c12 c13 c33 c44 minelastic (4 cells) 441.69 94.39 59.20 434.52 125.84 six single strains (12 cells) 441.65 94.41 59.15 434.52 125.79

The two agree to 0.05 GPa with a third of the calculations, and both agree with ABINIT's own density-functional perturbation theory (DFPT) tensor to 0.6 GPa.

The forces in the same four cells also give the internal-strain tensor, the force on each atom per unit strain, without further calculations:

The relaxed-ion constants need the ions relaxed in each strained cell, or a few more single points with displaced atoms; both are described in Relaxed-ion constants.

docs.title: First run with CP2K
docs.text: CP2K is driven through ASE's CP2K calculator, so the whole calculation is one Python script, with no input templates or output files to handle. Here we compute the clamped- and relaxed-ion elastic constants of silicon in a 64-atom cubic supercell at the \(\Gamma\) point. The output shown below is from this run.

docs.title: 1. Connect ASE to CP2K
docs.text:
ASE's calculator talks to CP2K's interactive shell, which current CP2K versions start with cp2k.psmp --shell. ASE requires the string cp2k_shell in the command, so the shell is started from a small script with that name. Every MPI rank reads the shell commands, so srun must pass the standard input to all tasks, which is its default:

#!/bin/bash
# file: cp2k_shell
exec srun -u -n "$SLURM_NTASKS" cp2k.psmp --shell "$@"

Make it executable (chmod +x cp2k_shell) and run the Python script below inside a Slurm job.

docs.title: 2. The script
docs.text:
import os

from ase.build import bulk
from ase.calculators.cp2k import CP2K
from ase.units import Ry

import minelastic

data = "/path/to/cp2k/data"           # the directory with CP2K's BASIS_MOLOPT and GTH_POTENTIALS
inp = """&FORCE_EVAL
  &DFT
    &SCF
      EPS_SCF 1.0E-8
      &OT
        MINIMIZER DIIS
        PRECONDITIONER FULL_ALL
        ENERGY_GAP 0.05
      &END OT
      &OUTER_SCF
        EPS_SCF 1.0E-8
        MAX_SCF 20
      &END OUTER_SCF
    &END SCF
    &MGRID
      REL_CUTOFF 60
    &END MGRID
  &END DFT
&END FORCE_EVAL
"""
calc = CP2K(command=os.path.abspath("cp2k_shell"), xc="PBE", cutoff=500 * Ry, max_scf=40,
            basis_set="DZVP-MOLOPT-SR-GTH", pseudo_potential="GTH-PBE",
            basis_set_file=f"{data}/BASIS_MOLOPT", potential_file=f"{data}/GTH_POTENTIALS",
            stress_tensor=True, inp=inp)

si = bulk("Si", "diamond", a=5.468, cubic=True).repeat(2)          # 64 atoms
result = minelastic.calculate(si, calc, ionic=True, stencil="central")
print(result.summary())

The calculator uses PBE with GTH pseudopotentials, the DZVP-MOLOPT-SR-GTH basis, a density cutoff of 500 Ry and a tight SCF threshold; stress_tensor=True makes CP2K compute the stress. This run uses \(a\) = 5.468 Å; relax the lattice parameter with the same calculator first.

Convergence

Elastic constants are differences of stresses of a few GPa, so they are much more sensitive to the density cutoff, the basis set, the supercell size (or k-point mesh) and the SCF threshold than total energies are. The settings here are chosen to show the workflow; they are not the result of a convergence study. Before using the constants in a publication, check that they change by less than the accuracy you need when the cutoff is raised and the basis and supercell are enlarged, and relax the reference structure with the final settings.

calculate finds the symmetry (cubic, one strain pattern), builds every strained cell, computes its stress with CP2K and returns the result. ionic=True adds cells in which one atom is displaced, which give the relaxed-ion constants without relaxing anything. stencil="central" applies each strain and displacement at two amplitudes instead of the default four, which halves the number of CP2K calculations.

docs.title: Your first elastic tensor
docs.text: Here we compute the elastic constants of copper with EMT, a simple interatomic potential that comes with ASE. The calculation takes a few seconds on a laptop and needs nothing besides minelastic, yet the steps are those of a DFT calculation: a relaxed reference structure, the strain set its symmetry requires, the stresses of the strained cells, and the constants.

docs.title: 1. Relax the reference structure
docs.text:
The elastic constants are derivatives of the stress at the equilibrium structure, so the cell is relaxed first, with the same calculator:

from ase.build import bulk
from ase.calculators.emt import EMT
from ase.filters import FrechetCellFilter
from ase.optimize import BFGS

atoms = bulk("Cu", "fcc", a=3.6, cubic=True)
atoms.calc = EMT()
BFGS(FrechetCellFilter(atoms), logfile=None).run(fmax=1e-6)
print(f"a = {atoms.cell[0, 0]:.4f} A")

a = 3.5898 A

docs.title: 2. Look at the strain set
docs.text:
ElasticSetup finds the symmetry of the structure and the strains that it needs:

import minelastic

setup = minelastic.ElasticSetup(atoms)
print(setup.describe())

space group Fm-3m (225), point group m-3m, elastic type cubic
3 independent constants: c11, c12, c44
invariant strains (free lattice parameters) = minimum number of strain patterns: 1
stiffness matrix in the working frame:
c11  c12  c12    0    0    0
c12  c11  c12    0    0    0
c12  c12  c11    0    0    0
  0    0    0  c44    0    0
  0    0    0    0  c44    0
  0    0    0    0    0  c44
strain set 'minimal': 1 pattern(s), step 0.01, multipliers (-2, -1, 1, 2)
  pattern 1: xx+yz          s1 = 1 c11, s2 = 1 c12, s3 = 1 c12, s4 = 1 c44

A cubic crystal has three independent elastic constants, and one strain pattern determines all of them. The pattern xx+yz stretches the cell along x and shears it in the yz plane at the same time. The relations on the last line say which stress component gives which constant: the stress \(\sigma_{xx}\) (s1) equals \(c_{11}\) times the strain, \(\sigma_{yy}\) and \(\sigma_{zz}\) (s2, s3) give \(c_{12}\), and the shear stress \(\sigma_{yz}\) (s4) gives \(c_{44}\). The usual approach applies six separate strains instead.

The pattern is applied at four strains, \(-0.02\), \(-0.01\), \(+0.01\) and \(+0.02\), and the stresses are differentiated numerically. These are the four strained cells:

for state in setup.states:
    print(state["id"], state["strain"])

s1_m1 [-0.01, -0.0, -0.0, -0.01, -0.0, -0.0]
s1_p1 [0.01, 0.0, 0.0, 0.01, 0.0, 0.0]
s1_p2 [0.02, 0.0, 0.0, 0.02, 0.0, 0.0]

The strains are written as six components in the order xx, yy, zz, yz, xz, xy, with the shear components as engineering strains (twice the tensor component).

docs.text:
calculate builds the strained cells, computes their stresses with the calculator and returns the result:

result = minelastic.calculate(atoms, EMT())
print(result.summary())

docs.title: 5. A crystal with internal relaxation
docs.text:
In hcp copper the atoms do not sit at centres of inversion, so a strain also moves them relative to the cell. The constants computed with the atoms held at their strained positions are the clamped-ion constants; the physical, relaxed-ion constants need the atoms relaxed in every strained cell, which relax_ions=True does:

hcp = bulk("Cu", "hcp", a=2.55, c=4.16)
hcp.calc = EMT()
BFGS(FrechetCellFilter(hcp), logfile=None).run(fmax=1e-6)

clamped = minelastic.calculate(hcp, EMT())
relaxed = minelastic.calculate(hcp, EMT(), relax_ions=True, fmax=1e-6)
for name in clamped.labels:
    print(f"{name}   clamped {clamped.as_dict()[name]:7.2f}   relaxed {relaxed.as_dict()[name]:7.2f}  GPa")

c11   clamped  233.60   relaxed  216.34  GPa
c12   clamped   94.81   relaxed  112.07  GPa
c13   clamped   74.77   relaxed   74.77  GPa
c33   clamped  254.00   relaxed  254.00  GPa
c44   clamped   49.30   relaxed   49.30  GPa

The hexagonal crystal has five constants and needs two strain patterns, 8 strained cells in place of the 24 of the six single strains. The relaxation changes c11 and c12 by 17 GPa and leaves the other constants unchanged.

The same steps with a DFT code are in the tutorials for VASP, Quantum ESPRESSO, ABINIT and CP2K.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
minelastic requires Python 3.9 or newer. Its dependencies, numpy, spglib and ASE, are installed with it:

pip install git+https://github.com/utksi/minelastic.git

The command-line tool is called minelastic. To check the installation:

$ minelastic --version
0.1.0

minelastic --help lists the commands, and minelastic generate --help the options of one of them.

docs.title: From a clone
docs.text:
The repository also contains the example scripts, the input templates of the tutorials and the tests:

git clone https://github.com/utksi/minelastic.git
cd minelastic
pip install -e ".[test]"
pytest tests

The tests take about a minute and need no DFT code: they use stored stresses of real calculations.

docs.title: Optional packages
docs.text: The DFT codes are not needed to install minelastic, to write the inputs or to read the results; they are needed only to run the calculations. Machine-learned potentials are used through their ASE calculators, for example pip install mace-torch for MACE. The tutorial with ASE's EMT potential relaxes the cell with ase.filters.FrechetCellFilter, which needs ASE 3.23 or newer. The documentation is built with pip install -e ".[docs]" followed by mkdocs serve.

docs.title: First run with Quantum ESPRESSO
docs.text: Here we compute the five elastic constants of wurtzite AlN with pw.x, starting from the input files of the relaxed structure. This takes four single-point calculations, 9 s in total on one 32-core node. The output shown below is from these runs.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the template
docs.text:
minelastic writes the input of every strained cell from a template: the pw.x input of the relaxed reference structure. We use examples/qe_aln/pw.in from the repository:

&CONTROL
  calculation = 'scf'
  prefix = 'aln'
  pseudo_dir = './pseudo'
  outdir = './tmp'
/
&SYSTEM
  ibrav = 4, celldm(1) = 5.911804, celldm(3) = 1.603472
  nat = 4, ntyp = 2
  ecutwfc = 50, ecutrho = 400
  occupations = 'fixed'
/
&ELECTRONS
  conv_thr = 1.0d-10
/
&IONS
/
ATOMIC_SPECIES
Al 26.982 Al.pbe-n-kjpaw_psl.1.0.0.UPF
N  14.007 N.pbe-n-kjpaw_psl.1.0.0.UPF
ATOMIC_POSITIONS crystal
Al 0.3333333333 0.6666666667 0.0000
Al 0.6666666667 0.3333333333 0.5000
N  0.3333333333 0.6666666667 0.3818
N  0.6666666667 0.3333333333 0.8818
K_POINTS automatic
8 8 5 0 0 0

It uses the PBE functional and the PAW potentials Al.pbe-n-kjpaw_psl.1.0.0.UPF and N.pbe-n-kjpaw_psl.1.0.0.UPF of pslibrary 1.0.0, with tight cutoffs and convergence threshold; the structure was relaxed with these settings.

Pseudopotential path

Every calculation runs in a directory of its own, so set pseudo_dir to the absolute path of the directory with the pseudopotential files.

Convergence

Elastic constants are differences of stresses of a few GPa, so they are much more sensitive to the cutoffs, the k-point mesh, the smearing and the convergence threshold than total energies are. The settings here are chosen to show the workflow; they are not the result of a convergence study. Before using the constants in a publication, check that they change by less than the accuracy you need when the cutoffs are raised and the k-point mesh refined, and relax the reference structure with the final settings.

The crystal is hexagonal, with five independent elastic constants, and two strain patterns determine all of them. Pattern 1 stretches the cell along x and shears it in the yz plane at the same time; pattern 2 stretches it along z. The entry s1 = 1 c11 means that the first stress component of pattern 1, \(\sigma_{xx}\), equals \(c_{11}\) times the strain. Every constant appears alone in at least one stress component, so each is read off directly.

Two points per strain

docs.title: 3. Write the inputs

$ minelastic generate qe qe_aln/pw.in -o el --stencil central
...
4 calculations written to el/ (list in el/STATES)

s1_m1

s2_m1

docs.title: 4. Run pw.x
docs.text:
The four calculations are independent. Run them one after another,

for d in $(cat el/STATES); do (cd el/$d && mpirun pw.x -in pw.in > pw.out); done

or at the same time, for example as a Slurm job array:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --array=1-4
d=el/$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" el/STATES)
cd "$d" && srun pw.x -in pw.in > pw.out

docs.title: First run with VASP
docs.text: Here we compute the five elastic constants of wurtzite AlN with VASP, starting from the input files of the relaxed structure. This takes four single-point calculations, 42 s in total on one 32-core node. The output shown below is from these runs.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the template
docs.text:
minelastic writes the input of every strained cell from a template: a directory with the VASP input of the relaxed reference structure. We use examples/vasp_aln from the repository. Copy the directory and add a PBE POTCAR for Al and N, in the order of the POSCAR. The INCAR is

PREC = Accurate
ENCUT = 520
EDIFF = 1E-8
ISMEAR = 0
SIGMA = 0.05
LREAL = .FALSE.
LWAVE = .FALSE.
LCHARG = .FALSE.

and the KPOINTS file asks for a Gamma-centred 8 x 8 x 5 mesh. The cutoff is 1.3 times the largest ENMAX of the POTCAR (520 eV for N), the electronic convergence is tight, real-space projection is off, and the structure in the POSCAR was relaxed with these settings.

Convergence

Elastic constants are differences of stresses of a few GPa, so they are much more sensitive to the plane-wave cutoff, the k-point mesh, the smearing and the electronic convergence than total energies are. The settings here are chosen to show the workflow; they are not the result of a convergence study. collect reads the stress of each cell from vasprun.xml and prints:

  • the five independent constants and the full stiffness matrix, in GPa, with \(C_{66} = (c_{11} - c_{12})/2\);
  • the Born stability test: the crystal is mechanically stable if all eigenvalues of the matrix are positive;
  • the Voigt-Reuss-Hill bulk modulus K, shear modulus G and Young's modulus E, Poisson's ratio nu and the universal anisotropy index A_U;
  • a consistency check: the stress components that are not needed for the constants are compared with the values that the fitted tensor predicts. A deviation of more than a few tenths of a GPa points to an unrelaxed reference structure, loose convergence or a lower symmetry than assumed.

docs.title: 7. Check the result
docs.text:
The same calculation with the six single strains (--scheme asess, 12 cells) and VASP's own finite differences (IBRION = 6, ISIF = 3, 12 cells) give, with the same settings:

docs.title: Elastic constants in practice
docs.text: The tutorials go through the basic workflow. Here we discuss the choices that determine the accuracy and the cost of the constants; the formulas are in the theory section, under Elastic constants.

docs.title: Prepare the reference structure
docs.text:
The elastic constants are derivatives of the stress at the stress-free equilibrium structure. Relax the reference structure with the same settings (functional, cutoff, k-point mesh, smearing) that the strained cells will use. The stresses of the strained cells differ from it by about \(\delta C\), 1 to 5 GPa for the default step \(\delta = 0.01\), so a residual stress of 0.1 GPa is harmless; it cancels in the difference to first order.

The same reasoning sets the accuracy the calculations need. In VASP, raise ENCUT to 1.3 to 1.4 times the largest ENMAX of the POTCAR, so that the Pulay stress changes little with the cell volume, and converge the electronic structure tightly (EDIFF of 1E-8). minelastic generate vasp reports the settings that the template does not meet (VASP). All strained cells use the k-point mesh of the template; a KSPACING in the INCAR is replaced by the explicit mesh of the reference cell.

One set of settings

Never combine cells computed with different codes or settings. The constants are differences of stresses, and a systematic difference between two cells does not cancel.

docs.title: Check the symmetry before running
docs.text:
minelastic info prints the space group, the elastic type and the number of strain patterns, without writing anything:

$ minelastic info --code vasp vasp_aln
space group P6_3mc (186), point group 6mm, elastic type hexagonal
...
strain set 'minimal': 2 pattern(s), step 0.01, multipliers (-2, -1, 1, 2)
...

If the space group is lower than expected, the structure is slightly distorted (symmetrize it, or pass a larger tolerance with --symprec, default 1e-5 Å), or magnetic order or different species labels lower the symmetry (Magnetic materials). The constants are still correct, but more cells are computed than necessary. A supercell whose lattice is less symmetric than the crystal also gets the strain set of the lower symmetry; start from the primitive or conventional cell.

docs.title: Choose the strain step and the number of points
docs.text:
Each strain pattern is applied at several multiples of the step \(\delta\), and the stresses are differentiated numerically. minelastic offers three finite-difference formulas, chosen with --stencil (stencil= in Python):

option strains error calculations per pattern four-point (default) \(\pm\delta\), \(\pm 2\delta\) of order \(\delta^4\) 4 central (default with --md) \(\pm\delta\) of order \(\delta^2\) 2 forward \(+\delta\) and the unstrained cell of order \(\delta\) 1 plus the reference

The four-point formula is the best choice for static calculations, where the stresses are precise and the error of the numerical derivative dominates. For hcp Cu (EMT), the two-point formula is off by 0.49 GPa at \(\delta = 0.01\). For wurtzite AlN in VASP, the minimal set and the six single strains differ by 0.14 GPa with two points and by 0.005 GPa with four. Averages over molecular dynamics are noisy, and the four-point weights \((1, -8, 8, -1)/12\) amplify that noise, so MD inputs use two points (Finite temperature).

The step --delta (default 0.01) should stay in the linear regime: 0.005 to 0.015 usually is. Smaller steps amplify numerical noise, larger ones add anharmonic contributions. For soft or strongly anharmonic materials, compare two steps.

docs.title: Check the result
docs.text:
The last line of the summary compares the stress components that are not needed for the constants with the values that the fitted tensor predicts:

consistency (redundant stress components): largest |computed - fitted| = 0.00 GPa (pattern 1, xz)

A deviation of more than a few tenths of a GPa points to a reference structure that is not relaxed, a strain step outside the linear regime, loose convergence, a k-point mesh that differs between cells, or a lower symmetry than assumed.

Two further checks cost more calculations. --scheme asess applies the six single strains, the usual approach, and should give the same constants within the error of the numerical derivative. collect --method lstsq fits all stress components of all patterns by least squares instead of reading each constant from the components that contain it alone (the default, uncoupled); a large change shows that some components are inconsistent.

docs.title: Orientation of the result
docs.text: The textbook constants (c11, c12, c13, c33, c44, ...) refer to the standard orientation of the crystal, for example the hexagonal c axis along z. If the stiffness matrix does not have its standard form in the input orientation, minelastic rotates the cell rigidly into the standard orientation before straining it, and reports the constants there. The full tensor in the input orientation is C_input_frame, in elastic.json and as result.C_input_frame. --frame input keeps the input orientation and --frame standard always rotates (Conventions).

docs.title: Compare with VASP's IBRION = 6
docs.text:
minelastic vasp-tensor OUTCAR reads the elastic tensor that VASP prints for IBRION = 6 and ISIF = 3, converts it to GPa and Voigt order and adds the stability test and the moduli:

minelastic vasp-tensor OUTCAR                     # TOTAL ELASTIC MODULI (relaxed ions)
minelastic vasp-tensor OUTCAR --which clamped     # SYMMETRIZED ELASTIC MODULI (clamped ions)

Its numbers differ from minelastic's by a few tenths of a GPa. VASP strains the cell by 0.015 (POTIM), applies simple shears instead of symmetric strains and differentiates \(J\sigma\), the stress times the volume ratio, instead of the stress itself. --delta 0.015 --stencil central --stress-measure kirchhoff --scheme asess comes closest to what VASP does with its default NFREE = 2.

docs.title: Use other strain sets
docs.text: Any set of patterns can be passed to ElasticSetup as scheme=[[...6 numbers...], ...], for example the strain sets tabulated by Le Page and Saxe. The constants are then fitted by least squares (method="lstsq"), since such sets are not uncoupled in general.

docs.title: Finite temperature
docs.text:
At a temperature \(T\) the elastic constants are the strain derivatives of the thermally averaged stress,

\[ C_{ij}(T) = \frac{\partial \langle \sigma_i \rangle_T}{\partial \varepsilon_j} , \]

taken at the thermally expanded lattice (theory). The strain sets are the same as at 0 K; only the stress of each strained cell becomes an average over a molecular-dynamics run. The saving is largest here, because every strained cell is a full MD run: a cubic crystal needs 2 runs instead of 12.

The protocol has three steps:

  1. an NPT run at zero pressure gives the lattice parameters at \(T\); most of the softening of the constants with temperature comes from thermal expansion;
  2. an NVT run with the cell held fixed in every strained cell of the expanded lattice (NPT would undo the strain);
  3. the constants from the averaged stresses, with standard errors from the fluctuations.

The stress fluctuations scale as \(1/\sqrt{N}\) with the number of atoms. A larger supercell, a longer run or a larger strain step (within the linear regime) reduce the error. MD inputs use two points per pattern, \(\pm\delta\), because the four-point formula amplifies the noise of the averages: at equal total MD time its result is about twice as noisy.

Metals

Use an electronic smearing that matches the temperature, in VASP ISMEAR = -1 with SIGMA = \(k_B T\).

docs.title: With an ASE calculator
docs.text:
examples/emt_finite_temperature.py follows the three steps for fcc Al with ASE's EMT potential in a 108-atom supercell. Berendsen NPT gives \(a(T)\). Langevin NVT then runs for 7000 steps of 2 fs (1000 of them for equilibration) in each of the two strained cells. The stresses include the kinetic part (include_ideal_gas=True) and are passed to ElasticSetup.compute as block averages, an array of samples per strain state:

setup = minelastic.ElasticSetup(bulk("Al", "fcc", a=a_T, cubic=True).repeat(3), delta=0.01, stencil="central")
stresses = {}
for st in setup.states:
    atoms = setup.strained_atoms(st)
    ...
    stresses[st["id"]] = s.reshape(-1, BLOCK, 6).mean(axis=1)
res = setup.compute(stresses)

s1_p1: 6000 steps, <stress> = [ 0.425  0.259  0.253  0.303  0.002 -0.009] GPa

c11        53.3     46.7 +- 0.4  GPa
c12        32.9     31.5 +- 0.5  GPa
c44        36.2     30.3 +- 0.4  GPa

The run takes a few minutes on one core.

Note

EMT is a toy potential for Al: only the workflow carries over, not the numbers.

docs.title: With VASP or Quantum ESPRESSO
docs.text:
The template is the NVT run of the thermally expanded supercell. generate --md keeps its MD settings and fixes the cell. For VASP, for example Langevin NVT at 600 K:

IBRION = 0 ; NSW = 10000 ; POTIM = 2
MDALGO = 3 ; LANGEVIN_GAMMA = 10 ; TEBEG = 600 ; TEEND = 600   # one LANGEVIN_GAMMA per species
ISMEAR = -1 ; SIGMA = 0.0517              # k_B T at 600 K (eV), for a metal

minelastic generate vasp ref_600K -o el_600K --md      # sets ISIF = 2 (fixed cell), keeps IBRION, NSW, POTIM
# run the MD in every directory of el_600K/STATES
minelastic collect el_600K --md --skip 1000 --kinetic-temperature 600

--skip discards the equilibration steps. VASP and pw.x print the stress without its kinetic part, and --kinetic-temperature adds it (\(n k_B T\) in \(C_{11}\), \(C_{12}\), ..., about 0.25 GPa for Al at 300 K). For pw.x, the template has calculation = 'md' with a thermostat in &IONS and a fixed cell, and the rest is the same. minelastic refuses to collect MD runs without --md (or --samples), so that the last step is never taken by mistake.

Error bars

The standard errors assume uncorrelated steps. Thin or block-average the trajectory if you need reliable error bars.

A cheaper route runs the MD with a machine-learned force field and computes accurate single points on selected snapshots, in sub-directories conf-* of each strain state. Collect them with

minelastic collect el_600K --samples 'conf-*'

This works with every interface. The paper uses this protocol for fcc Al from 300 to 900 K: ab initio MD in a 108-atom supercell, accelerated by on-the-fly machine-learned force fields.

The constants from fixed-cell NVT runs are isothermal. Ultrasonic experiments measure adiabatic constants, which differ in c11 and c12 of a cubic crystal (through the bulk modulus) but not in c44 (theory).

docs.title: Internal strain and force constants
docs.text:
The internal-strain tensor is the force on each atom per unit strain, with the atoms held at their strained fractional positions,

\[ \Lambda_{n\alpha, J} = \frac{\partial F_{n\alpha}}{\partial \varepsilon_J} \]

for atom \(n\), Cartesian direction \(\alpha\) and strain component \(J\), in eV/Å. It describes how the atoms move when the crystal is strained, and it enters the relaxed-ion elastic constants and the piezoelectric tensor (theory).

minelastic obtains \(\Lambda\) in two ways. The forces in the strained cells give it without further calculations: by symmetry, the few patterns of the minimal set determine the whole tensor. With --ionic, the stresses of cells with displaced atoms give it a second time, together with the \(\Gamma\)-point force constants \(\Phi_{m\alpha, n\beta} = -\partial F_{m\alpha}/\partial u_{n\beta}\) in eV/Å\(^2\).

docs.title: With an ASE calculator
docs.text:
examples/emt_internal_strain.py computes both routes for hcp Cu with EMT. ionic=True adds the cells with displaced atoms:

from ase.build import bulk
from ase.calculators.emt import EMT
import minelastic

res = minelastic.calculate(bulk("Cu", "hcp", a=2.55, c=4.16), EMT(), ionic=True)
print(res.internal_strain.shape)              # Lambda from the strained cells, (N, 3, 6), eV/A
print(res.internal_strain_displaced.shape)    # Lambda from the displaced atoms
print(res.force_constants.shape)              # Phi, (N, 3, N, 3), eV/A^2
print(res.ionic_relaxation.shape)             # Phi^+ Lambda, (N, 3, 6), A per unit strain

(2, 3, 6)
(2, 3, 6)
(2, 3, 2, 3)
(2, 3, 6)

The script compares both tensors with brute force, the forces of all atoms under each of the six single strains:

...

[[ 0.      0.     -0.      0.      0.     -1.9159]

The two patterns of the minimal set determine the whole tensor, and the predicted relaxation of the atoms per unit strain, \(u = \Phi^+ \Lambda\), is the one that relaxing the atoms gives.

for d in $(cat el/STATES); do (cd el/$d && mpirun vasp_std > out); done

$ minelastic collect el --internal-strain
...
internal strain tensor dF/de (eV/A), columns xx yy zz yz xz xy:
  ion   1 x    -0.0000     0.0000     0.0000    -0.0000    -4.9075    -8.2521

The tensor has the sign and units of the one that VASP prints for IBRION = 6 (INTERNAL STRAIN TENSOR FOR ION), which VASP computes from displaced atoms:

Al (ion 1), eV/Å z, zz x, xy x, xz z, xx minelastic, 4 strained cells 11.095 -8.252 -4.908 -5.080 VASP IBRION = 6 11.130 -8.243 -4.897 -5.084

The largest difference over all atoms and components is 0.04 eV/Å. With --ionic, the tensor from the displaced atoms agrees with VASP's to 0.06 eV/Å, and the force constants are written to elastic.json (force_constants_eV_per_A2).

docs.title: With Quantum ESPRESSO and other codes
docs.text: pw.x forces are read from the same output as the stresses (generate switches tprnfor on), and the Quantum ESPRESSO and ABINIT tutorials end with the tensor. For wurtzite AlN with pw.x, the tensors from the minimal set and from the six single strains agree to 0.007 eV/Å. Every interface that returns forces gives the tensor; with your own calculations, pass the forces as compute(stresses, forces={state_id: (N, 3) array}) (Your own workflow).

docs.title: Magnetic materials
docs.text:
Magnetic order can lower the symmetry of a crystal, and with it the form of the elastic tensor and the strain set. minelastic uses the magnetic space group (from spglib), including the operations combined with time reversal, which also constrain the internal-strain and piezoelectric tensors. Rocksalt NiO, for example, is cubic without magnetic order, but its AFM-I order, ferromagnetic (001) planes of Ni with alternating moments, makes it tetragonal:

from ase.build import bulk
import minelastic

nio = bulk("NiO", "rocksalt", a=4.17, cubic=True)
print(minelastic.ElasticSetup(nio).describe().splitlines()[0])

z = nio.get_scaled_positions()[:, 2]
moments = [(2.0 if zi < 0.25 else -2.0) if s == "Ni" else 0.0
           for s, zi in zip(nio.get_chemical_symbols(), z)]
nio.set_initial_magnetic_moments(moments)
setup = minelastic.ElasticSetup(nio)
print(setup.describe().splitlines()[0])
print(len(setup.patterns), "strain patterns:", setup.form.labels)

space group Fm-3m (225), point group m-3m, elastic type cubic
space group P4/mmm (123), point group 4/mmm, elastic type tetragonal-II
2 strain patterns: ['c11', 'c12', 'c13', 'c33', 'c44', 'c66']

There are six constants and two strain patterns instead of three and one. The difference matters: in DFT calculations of NiO AFM-I with VASP, pw.x and ABINIT, c11 and c33 differ by 33 to 40 GPa, which the cubic form, used if the moments were ignored, would miss (Validation).

docs.title: Where the moments come from
docs.text:
The initial moments are read from the template:

code moments used for the symmetry VASP MAGMOM when ISPIN = 2, LNONCOLLINEAR or LSORBIT is set (collinear as scalars, noncollinear as axial vectors) ABINIT spinat: the z components with nsppol 2 or nspden 2, the vectors with nspden 4 pw.x the species labels; with noncolin, also the directions from starting_magnetization, angle1, angle2 FHI-aims, ASE the initial magnetic moments of the structure (initial_moment in geometry.in)

Check the space group that minelastic info prints before running anything.

docs.title: Points to watch
docs.text:
A collinear pw.x run distinguishes the magnetic sublattices by their species labels, as pw.x requires, but then the operations that exchange them together with a spin flip are not used. An antiferromagnet such as MnF2 then gets the orthorhombic set of 3 patterns instead of the tetragonal set of 2; the constants are the same, at the cost of more cells.

ASE calculators

With an ASE calculator, the moments of the structure must be those the calculator uses. EMT and MACE ignore them, and ASE's CP2K calculator has no per-atom moments.

If the cell has to be rotated to its standard orientation, noncollinear inputs are refused, because the moment directions would have to be rotated too. Use --frame input (frame="input") to keep the input orientation.

docs.title: Your own workflow
docs.text: The command line covers the usual case: write the inputs, run them, read the outputs. The Python API lets you replace any of these steps, for example to run the calculations with a workflow manager, with a code that minelastic has no interface for, or with stresses that you already have.

docs.title: Bring your own stresses
docs.text:
ElasticSetup lists the strain states of a structure and builds their cells, and compute turns the stresses into the elastic tensor. How the stresses are computed is up to you:

from ase.build import bulk
from ase.calculators.emt import EMT
from ase.units import GPa
from minelastic import ElasticSetup


def my_code_stress(atoms):
    """Stand-in for your own calculation: Cauchy stress in GPa, tension positive, Voigt xx yy zz yz xz xy."""
    atoms.calc = EMT()
    return atoms.get_stress(voigt=True) / GPa


setup = ElasticSetup(bulk("Cu", "fcc", a=3.5898, cubic=True))
stresses = {}
for state in setup.states:                         # state["id"] = 's1_m2', 's1_m1', ...
    cell = setup.strained_atoms(state)             # ASE Atoms of this strained cell
    stresses[state["id"]] = my_code_stress(cell)
result = setup.compute(stresses)
print({name: round(value, 2) for name, value in result.as_dict().items()})

{'c11': 172.62, 'c12': 115.44, 'c44': 89.91}

Compute the stress of each cell exactly as strained_atoms returns it: the cell may have been rotated into the standard orientation of the crystal (Conventions). compute also takes the forces of the cells (forces={state_id: (N, 3) array} in eV/Å) for the internal-strain tensor, and their dipoles (polarization={state_id: (3,) array} in e Å) for the piezoelectric tensor.

res = setup.compute(data["stress_GPa"], polarization=data["dipole_eA"])

docs.title: Save and restore a setup
docs.text:
When the calculations run for days, store the setup and rebuild it later. to_dict returns a JSON-ready record, the one that generate writes to minelastic.json, and from_dict rebuilds the same strain states from it:

import json

with open("setup.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(setup.to_dict(), f)
with open("setup.json") as f:
    restored = ElasticSetup.from_dict(json.load(f))
print(restored.compute(stresses).as_dict() == result.as_dict())

True

docs.title: Drive a DFT code from Python
docs.text:
minelastic.generate and minelastic.collect are the functions behind the two commands, so a VASP, Quantum ESPRESSO or ABINIT workflow can be scripted without the command line. With the template of the VASP tutorial:

import minelastic

setup, notes = minelastic.generate("vasp", "vasp_aln", "el", stencil="central")
print(len(setup.states), "calculations")
for note in notes:
    print("NOTE:", note)

4 calculations
NOTE: INCAR: set IBRION = -1, NSW = 0, ISIF = 2

After the runs, collect reads the results and writes el/elastic.json:

result = minelastic.collect("el")
print({name: round(value, 2) for name, value in result.as_dict().items()})

{'c11': 440.26, 'c12': 96.78, 'c13': 62.16, 'c33': 432.32, 'c44': 125.02}

The keyword arguments are the options of the commands (Python API).

docs.title: Born charges and piezoelectricity
docs.text:
The piezoelectric stress tensor is the change of the polarization with strain, and the strain coefficients follow with the compliance \(S = C^{-1}\):

\[ e_{iJ} = \frac{\partial P_i}{\partial \varepsilon_J} \quad (\mathrm{C/m^2}), \qquad d = e\, S \quad (\mathrm{pC/N}). \]

The Born effective charges \(Z^*_{n,\alpha\beta} = \partial p_\alpha / \partial u_{n\beta}\) are the change of the dipole \(p\) of the cell when atom \(n\) moves (theory).

minelastic takes the polarization of every cell from its dipole, for example from a Berry-phase calculation. The strained cells alone give the clamped-ion tensor \(e^0\), with no further calculations if the dipoles are computed with the stresses. With --ionic, the displaced atoms add the Born charges, and the relaxed-ion (total) tensor follows as \(e = e^0 + Z^* \Phi^+ \Lambda / \Omega\), together with the relaxed-ion elastic constants and \(d\).

docs.title: With an ASE calculator
docs.text:
calculate takes the dipole as a function of the Atoms of each cell, returning the dipole in e Å. examples/bks_quartz_piezo.py uses the BKS rigid-ion model of silica (charges \(q_{Si} = 2.4\), \(q_O = -1.2\) and Buckingham terms, as a small ASE calculator in the script) for alpha-quartz, point group 32. In a rigid-ion model the dipole is \(p = \sum_n q_n r_n\):

def dipole(a):
    return q @ a.positions

ionic = minelastic.calculate(atoms, BKS(), ionic=True, dipole=dipole, delta=0.005, displacement=0.005)
relaxed = minelastic.calculate(atoms, BKS(), relax_ions=True, fmax=1e-7, steps=4000, dipole=dipole, delta=0.005)

The results are ionic.born (\(Z^*\)), ionic.piezo (\(e^0\)), ionic.piezo_total (\(e\)) and ionic.piezo_d (\(d\)). In a rigid-ion model \(Z^*\) equals the charges and \(e^0 = 0\): the whole response comes from the relaxation of the ions. docs.title: Clamped-ion tensor from the strained cells alone
docs.text:
Without --ionic, collect --piezo on clamped cells computed with LCALCPOL gives the clamped-ion tensor \(e^0\) from the same 4 cells as the elastic constants: the polarization of the few strained cells determines the whole tensor by symmetry. For this AlN example, e33 = -0.428 C/m\(^2\), against -0.424 C/m\(^2\) from DFPT; examples/replay_vasp_aln.py reproduces it from the stored stresses and dipoles.

Berry phase and relaxations

VASP evaluates the Berry phase only for the first ionic step. In a relaxation the dipole would belong to the unrelaxed structure, so minelastic refuses dipoles from relaxed-ion cells; the total tensor comes from --ionic, which needs single points only.

docs.title: With other codes
docs.text: The elastic part of --ionic (force constants, internal strain, relaxed-ion constants) works with every interface. minelastic reads Berry-phase dipoles from VASP output only. With other codes, pass the dipoles (in e Å, physical sign) to ElasticSetup.compute(stresses, forces=..., polarization={state_id: dipole}), or \(Z^*\) and \(e^0\) from a perturbation-theory run with born= and clamped_piezo= (Your own workflow).

docs.title: Relaxed-ion constants
docs.text:
When a crystal is strained, atoms that are not fixed by symmetry move inside the cell. The constants with the atoms held at their strained fractional positions are the clamped-ion constants \(C^0\). Experiments measure the relaxed-ion constants, because at acoustic frequencies the atoms follow the strain:

\[ C = C^0 - \frac{1}{\Omega}\, \Lambda^{\mathsf T} \Phi^{+} \Lambda , \]

lowered by the relaxation of the atoms. Here \(\Lambda\) is the internal-strain tensor (force on each atom per unit strain), \(\Phi\) the \(\Gamma\)-point force constants and \(\Omega\) the cell volume (theory).

Info

If every atom sits at a centre of inversion, as in fcc, bcc, rocksalt or cubic perovskites, nothing relaxes and \(C = C^0\).

minelastic computes \(C\) in two ways:

relax the ions displace the atoms option --relax-ions, relax_ions=True --ionic, ionic=True calculations one relaxation per strained cell one single point per strained cell, plus one per symmetry-irreducible atomic displacement and step also gives the force constants and, with dipoles, the Born charges and piezoelectric tensors watch out for relaxations must be converged tightly: a strain of 0.01 induces forces of only about 0.05 eV/Å an unstable or soft optical mode makes the relaxed-ion response undefined; minelastic stops with an error

The second route is the linear response itself, the method of VASP's IBRION = 6. It needs no relaxations, which makes it cheaper and more robust in most cases. The two routes differ by terms of second order in the strain step.

VASP's own IBRION = 6 uses the same 8 displaced cells but 12 strained cells, because it always applies the six single strains. For the template of the VASP tutorial, with two points per strain:

docs.title: With other codes
docs.text: Both routes work with every interface. With ABINIT, --relax-ions appends ionmov 2, ntime 100 and tolmxf 1.0d-6 unless the input sets ionmov; with FHI-aims, it adds relax_geometry bfgs 1E-3. With CP2K through ASE, ionic=True lowers c44 of diamond Si from the clamped-ion 102.6 GPa to 79.7 GPa (CP2K tutorial).

docs.title: info shows more strain patterns than expected
docs.text: The number of patterns follows from the symmetry that spglib finds with the tolerance symprec (default 1e-5 Å). A slightly distorted structure is found with a lower symmetry: symmetrize it, or pass a larger --symprec. Magnetic order can also lower the symmetry (Magnetic materials), as can atoms of one element in different VASP species blocks or with different pw.x species labels, which minelastic treats as different species, as the DFT code does. spglib lists only the operations that map the lattice of the given cell onto itself, so a supercell whose lattice is less symmetric than the crystal gets the set of that lower symmetry. In all these cases the constants are still correct, but more cells are computed than necessary.

docs.title: The consistency check reports a large deviation
docs.text: The stress components that are not used for the constants disagree with the fitted tensor. Possible causes are a structure of lower symmetry than assumed (see above), a strain step outside the linear regime, too loose electronic or ionic convergence, a k-point mesh that differs between cells, or the noise of MD averages. collect --method lstsq shows how much the constants depend on which stress components are used.

docs.title: The constants differ from VASP's IBRION = 6
docs.text: By a few tenths of a GPa, because the numerical derivatives differ: VASP strains the cell by 0.015, applies simple shears and differentiates the stress times the volume ratio (Elastic constants in practice). Differences of several GPa point to different settings: VASP's IBRION = 6 run may use another cutoff, k-point mesh or PREC than the template.

docs.title: collect refuses to read MD runs
docs.text: Without --md, minelastic reads the stress of the last ionic step only. So that the last step of an MD run is never taken by mistake, collect stops if the inputs were written with generate --md; collect them with --md --skip N (or --samples for snapshots).

docs.title: --ionic stops with an unstable or soft mode
docs.text: The force constants have a negative or nearly zero eigenvalue besides the three uniform translations. The relaxed-ion response is then undefined: the reference structure is not at a minimum of the energy, or a phonon at \(\Gamma\) is unstable. Relax the atoms of the reference structure tightly, and check the structure.

docs.title: Noncollinear inputs are refused
docs.text: The cell had to be rotated into the standard orientation of the crystal, and the moment directions (and other direction-dependent inputs such as SAXIS, EFIELD or Cartesian k points) would have to be rotated with it. Use --frame input to keep the input orientation.

docs.title: Can I combine cells from different codes or settings?
docs.text: No. All strained cells of a set must be computed with identical settings. The constants are differences of stresses, and systematic differences between cells do not cancel.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
import minelastic
from minelastic import ElasticSetup, ElasticResult, calculate, generate, collect

All quantities follow the conventions: GPa, Voigt order xx yy zz yz xz xy, engineering shear strain, stress positive in tension.

name what it does calculate the whole calculation with an ASE calculator, in memory ElasticSetup the strain set of a structure, its strained cells, and the tensor from their stresses ElasticResult the constants, tensors, moduli and checks generate, collect the minelastic generate and minelastic collect commands, for DFT codes

Builds ElasticSetup(atoms, **setup_kwargs), computes the stress (eV/A^3 from calc, converted to GPa, tension positive) and the forces (eV/A) of every state with calc, and returns ElasticSetup.compute of them.

docs.title: ElasticSetup
docs.text:
Strain set of one crystal and the extraction of its elastic constants.

The point group of atoms restricts the stiffness to C = sum_p c_p B_p with n independent constants c_p. Each strain pattern u_k (a 6-vector, engineering Voigt) is applied at the strains m delta u_k for the multipliers m of the finite-difference formula.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default atoms Atoms

Reference structure, relaxed and stress-free for the textbook constants. Initial magnetic moments enter the symmetry analysis.

required scheme str or list

'minimal' (the minimal uncoupled set), 'asess' (the six single-component strains), or a list of 6-vectors (patterns per unit step, engineering Voigt).

'minimal' delta float

Strain step.

0.01 stencil str or tuple

'four-point' (multipliers -2, -1, 1, 2; error O(delta^4); the default), 'central' (-1, 1; error O(delta^2), half the cells, the choice for noisy MD averages), 'forward' (1, with the unstrained reference) or a tuple of multipliers of delta.

'four-point' symprec float

spglib tolerance (Angstrom).

1e-05 frame str

'auto', 'input' or 'standard': orientation in which the strains are applied (see _choose).

'auto' ionic bool

Also displace the symmetry-irreducible atoms, for the relaxed-ion and piezoelectric response from clamped calculations (see ionic.py).

False displacement float

Atomic step (Angstrom), with the same multipliers as the strains.

0.01

Attributes:

Name Type Description states list of dict

One dict per calculation, with id, pattern, amplitude and strain (engineering Voigt): 's{k}_p{m}' / 's{k}_m{m}' for pattern k at +m delta / -m delta, 'd{k}_p{m}' / 'd{k}_m{m}' for displacement k (with atom and the Cartesian vector in Angstrom), and 'ref' (zero strain) when the formula has no negative multiplier.

patterns (K, 6) array

The strain patterns u_k.

displacements list

The symmetry-irreducible (atom index, Cartesian unit vector) pairs, with ionic.

atoms, input_atoms, rotation

The reference structure in the working frame and as given, and the rotation R with x_work = R x_input.

symmetry

Space-group number, international symbol, point group, Cartesian rotations and atom permutations.

form TensorForm

The symmetry-adapted form of C: labels of the independent constants, matrix(c), project(C) and expression(i, j).

n_min int

Lower bound on the number of strain patterns: the dimension of the invariant strain subspace.

docs.title: compute
docs.text:
compute(
    stresses,
    forces=None,
    method="uncoupled",
    kinetic_temperature=None,
    stress_measure="cauchy",
    polarization=None,
    pol_quantum=1.0,
    born=None,
    clamped_piezo=None,
    internal_strain_from="displacements",
)

Elastic tensor from the stresses (and optionally forces and dipoles) of the states.

r_k = (1/delta) sum_m g_m sigma(m delta u_k) is the response of pattern k (of J sigma for 'kirchhoff', J = det F), and r_ki = sum_p a_kip c_p with a_kip = (B_p u_k)_i. 'uncoupled': c_p is the mean of r_ki / a_kip over all single-constant relations of p, with its standard error from Cov(r_k) (correlations within a pattern included); 'designated': the first such relation; 'lstsq': weighted least squares over all relations, weight w_i^2 / |u_k|_M^2 (Mandel stress metric, per unit Mandel strain of the pattern), or, with samples, generalized least squares with Cov(r_k). Then C = sum_p c_p B_p, plus n kB T in C_ij (i, j <= 3) for kinetic_temperature (Cauchy stress only: the Kirchhoff kinetic stress -N kB T / V0 does not depend on the strain). checks compares every r_ki with (C u_k)_i.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default stresses dict

{state_id: (6,) or (n_samples, 6)} Cauchy stress in GPa, physical sign (tension > 0), Voigt order xx yy zz yz xz xy, in the working frame (as computed for the generated cells). Several samples (e.g. MD configurations) are averaged and give standard errors.

required forces dict

{state_id: (N, 3)} forces (eV/A) of clamped-ion calculations, giving the internal-strain tensor.

None method str

'uncoupled' (every constant from the stress components that contain it alone, averaged over all such components), 'designated' (the first such component only, as in the paper's tables) or 'lstsq' (least squares over all stress components of all patterns).

'uncoupled' kinetic_temperature float

T (K): add the ideal-gas term n kB T to C_ij (i, j <= 3), for MD stresses that contain only the virial (e.g. VASP).

None stress_measure str

'cauchy' (default) differentiates the Cauchy stress; 'kirchhoff' differentiates J sigma (J = V/V0), as VASP does for IBRION=6 (SIF/Omega0). Both give the same constants for a stress-free reference; they differ at O(delta^2) in the finite differences.

'cauchy' polarization dict

{state_id: (3,)} dipole moment of the cell in e*Angstrom, physical sign (positive charge), e.g. from a Berry-phase calculation. Gives the proper piezoelectric tensor (clamped-ion for clamped cells, total for relaxed ions), completed by symmetry, and with ionic=True the Born charges.

None pol_quantum float

Berry-phase quantum in reduced units used for the branch alignment (1 is safe for spin-polarized and non-spin-polarized cases alike).

1.0 born array

With ionic=True: (N, 3, 3) Born charges (|e|, Z[n, alpha, j] = dp_alpha/du_nj, working frame), e.g. from DFPT; replaces those from the dipoles of the displaced atoms.

None clamped_piezo array

With ionic=True: (3, 6) clamped-ion piezoelectric tensor (C/m^2, working frame), e.g. from DFPT; used when the strained cells have no dipoles.

None internal_strain_from str

With ionic=True: 'displacements' (stresses of the displaced cells, as VASP, for the ionic terms) or 'strains' (forces in the strained cells).

'displacements'

docs.title: Units and notation
docs.text:
quantity unit convention stress \(\sigma\) GPa Cauchy stress, positive in tension; Voigt order xx, yy, zz, yz, xz, xy strain \(\varepsilon\) dimensionless Voigt order as above, engineering shear components (\(\varepsilon_4 = 2\varepsilon_{yz}\)) elastic constants \(C\) GPa 6x6 Voigt matrix, \(\sigma_i = \sum_j C_{ij} \varepsilon_j\) internal-strain tensor \(\Lambda\) eV/Å \(\Lambda[n, \alpha, J] = \partial F_{n\alpha} / \partial \varepsilon_J\) (per unit engineering strain) force constants \(\Phi\) eV/Å\(^2\) \(\Phi[m, \alpha, n, \beta] = -\partial F_{m\alpha} / \partial u_{n\beta}\) Born charges \(Z^*\) |e| \(Z[n, \alpha, j] = \partial p_\alpha / \partial u_{nj}\) piezoelectric stress tensor \(e\) C/m\(^2\) \(e_{iJ} = \partial P_i / \partial \varepsilon_J\), rows x, y, z, Voigt columns piezoelectric strain tensor \(d\) pC/N \(d = e S\), \(S = C^{-1}\) the relaxed-ion compliance dipoles (input to compute) e Å physical sign (positive charge)

The code readers convert on reading. VASP prints the stress in kB, pressure-like (positive in compression), in the order XX YY ZZ XY YZ ZX. pw.x prints Ry/bohr\(^3\), also pressure-like. ASE uses eV/Å\(^3\), positive in tension. The VASP elastic tensors (vasp-tensor) are converted from kBar to GPa and reordered to Voigt order.

docs.title: Strains
docs.text:
A strain is applied as the symmetric deformation gradient \(F = I + \varepsilon\) (no rigid rotation) to the lattice vectors, with the fractional coordinates fixed. Each pattern is applied at multiples of the step \(\delta\) (default 0.01) given by the stencil option:

  • four-point (default): \(\pm\delta\), \(\pm 2\delta\), weights \((1, -8, 8, -1)/12\delta\), error \(O(\delta^4)\);
  • central (the default for MD inputs, generate --md): \(\pm\delta\), error \(O(\delta^2)\), half the calculations;
  • forward: \(+\delta\) and the unstrained reference, error \(O(\delta)\).

The four-point formula makes the result independent of the strain set to within \(O(\delta^4)\), so the minimal set and the six single strains agree closely. For averages of noisy stresses (MD) it amplifies the noise; central differences are then the better choice.

The stress is differentiated as the Cauchy stress by default. stress_measure="kirchhoff" (--stress-measure kirchhoff) differentiates \(J\sigma\) instead, with \(J = V/V_0\), as VASP does for IBRION = 6. For a stress-free reference both give the same constants. They differ at \(O(\delta^2)\) in the finite differences.

docs.title: Orientation
docs.text:
The tensor form, and with it the strain set, depends on how the crystal axes lie in the Cartesian frame. minelastic derives the form from the point-group rotations of the given cell, so any orientation is handled correctly. The textbook constants (c11, c12, c13, c33, c44, ...) refer to the standard orientation, though. Examples of non-standard orientations are a hexagonal c axis along x, or a rhombohedral cell with its 3-fold axis along [111]. With frame="auto" (the default), minelastic keeps the input orientation if the stiffness matrix has its standard form there. Otherwise it rotates the cell rigidly into the spglib standard orientation, the working frame.

  • The constants, result.C and the strained cells refer to the working frame.
  • result.C_input_frame (and C_input_frame in elastic.json) is the full tensor rotated back to the input orientation.
  • frame="input" or "standard" forces one or the other.

For the trigonal space groups of type 312 (P312, P31m, P-31m and the others), the standard setting with a parallel to x has c15 instead of c14. minelastic handles both forms.

docs.title: Symmetry tolerance
docs.text: The symmetry is found by spglib with symprec = 1e-5 Å by default, the value VASP uses. Increase it (--symprec 1e-3) for structures relaxed with loose tolerances. The space group, the elastic type and the number of strain patterns are printed by minelastic info. If they are not what you expect, fix the structure (or the tolerance) before running anything.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: pytest tests runs the test suite in about 20 seconds. Nearly all of it runs on data shipped in tests/, so no DFT code is needed.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
• The paper's strain sets and extraction formulas are reproduced for all nine elastic types. Their minimality is confirmed by exhaustive search.
  • Random symmetry-adapted tensors are recovered exactly from synthetic stresses with nonlinear terms. This holds in standard and random orientations, for every extraction method, with the central and four-point formulas.
  • With ASE's EMT potential, the minimal and six-strain sets agree for clamped ions, relaxed ions and the internal-strain tensor.
  • The symmetry completion of the internal-strain, piezoelectric and force-constant tensors is exact. The completed EMT force constants equal those from displacing every atom (1e-8 eV/Å\(^2\)).
  • The internal-strain tensor of hcp Cu (EMT) from the two patterns of the minimal set equals brute force (all six single strains, all atoms) to 4e-5 eV/Å, and the tensor from the displaced atoms to 4e-6 eV/Å. The predicted relaxation per unit strain equals that of relaxing the atoms (examples/emt_internal_strain.py).
  • For alpha-quartz with the BKS rigid-ion model, the relaxed-ion constants and the piezoelectric tensor from clamped single points (ionic=True) equal those from relaxing the ions in the strained cells to 0.1 GPa and 2e-4 C/m\(^2\), and the Born charges equal the model charges (examples/bks_quartz_piezo.py).
  • The VASP and Quantum ESPRESSO writers and readers are tested. The pw.x lattice construction was also checked against pw.x's own output for every ibrav (1, 2, 3, -3, 4, 5, -5, 6 to 11, -9, 91, 12, -12, 13, -13 and 14, with celldm and with A, B, C).

docs.title: Real VASP data
docs.text: From the raw \(\pm\delta\) stresses of IBRION = 6 runs (tests/data), minelastic reproduces the tensors that VASP printed to 5e-5 GPa. This covers unmodified VASP and patched VASP builds that apply the minimal sets. The minimal and six-strain sets agree for AlN (0.14 GPa), Se in two orientations (up to 0.07 GPa) and Al (1.05 GPa with a 31x31x31 k-mesh).

docs.title: The paper's benchmark runs
docs.text:
tests/data_paper holds the stresses of the runs behind Table IV of the paper, one material per elastic type, plus CaWO4, Bi and BaTiO3:

elastic type material triclinic albite monoclinic β-Ga2O3 orthorhombic TiSi2 tetragonal I CaMoO4 tetragonal II rutile TiO2 trigonal I dolomite trigonal II α-quartz hexagonal Mg cubic Al

Each material has a run with VASP's six strains and a run with the paper's minimal set (a patched VASP). From the raw stresses, minelastic reproduces the clamped-ion tensor VASP printed. The six-strain runs agree exactly (below 1e-3 GPa). The minimal runs agree within 0.2 GPa, because the paper's implementation uses a different finite-difference estimator. With VASP's ionic relaxation term added, the results reproduce the published Table IV:

  • the eigenvalues agree within 0.2 GPa;
  • the individual constants agree within 0.16 GPa where the run frame is the paper's. For α-quartz the agreement is up to the sign of c14, which depends on how the a axes are placed.

The minimal and six-strain sets agree within 0.6 GPa (Al: 1.05 GPa). The β-Ga2O3 runs are sibling runs of the published ones, within about 2%.

The reference is VASP's own IBRION = 6 with LEPSILON, for wurtzite AlN (tests/data_ionic, tests/data_berry):

  • the clamped-ion piezoelectric tensor from the Berry-phase dipoles of the 4 minimal strained cells agrees with DFPT to 0.005 C/m\(^2\) (e33 = -0.424 C/m\(^2\)).
